analysis: The closest option has a sustained ancient material, literary and intellectual core: world and Greek archaeology, ancient Athenian democracy, empires and warfare, myth and major ancient works, political thought and rhetoric. Later-period literary, art-historical, media and historical methods complement this core without being described as further ancient content.

The heritage option emphasises museums, public history, documentary production, representation and material evidence. The political option retains ancient textual and archaeological anchors and gives more weight to institutions, conflict and historical comparison. Generic private and EU law are removed; classical literature, visual interpretation and reception gain weight. Both remain bounded interdisciplinary responses rather than specialist ancient-history or archaeology degrees.

Both offering conflicts are resolved through replacing school-based rhetoric teaching with philosophical interpretation of emotion and culture. Other replacements strengthen classical and cultural inquiry rather than using modern television history or generic legal courses. Every substantive contribution has been read against its profile or official description. The three programmes pass current offerings, prerequisites and pairwise distinctness.

Thirteen bounded positive alignments recognise meaningful primary content or methodological overlap without demanding identical scope. Specialist Near Eastern history, religion, textual-source training, excursion, open space and thesis preserve appropriate blanks. Optional research is outside the 180 EC.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: introduces legal traditions, social justice and legal reasoning as modern analytical perspectives on institutions and their historical interpretation

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: examines modern transformations and historical visions of the future, supporting study of how later societies frame and reuse the past

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.contribution: compares ancient Persia, Rome and China with later empires through institutions, legitimacy, cultural power and historical evidence

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.contribution: traces warfare from antiquity onward, using strategic texts and primary sources to test claims about Western power

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.contribution: examines Indigenous historical memory, dispossession and resurgence through reciprocal inquiry and public-history work; it supplies a comparative heritage perspective, not ancient Mediterranean history

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: develops historical research questions, source criticism and an independent paper in the American context; its contribution is historical method rather than ancient regional content

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: examines human-rights traditions, legal institutions and competing arguments about dignity and democracy, complementing historical study of political values

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.contribution: reads ancient Greek and later philosophical arguments about knowledge, ethics, identity and political questions

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: develops interpretation and evaluation of ethical theories, including ancient virtue ethics and later reinterpretations

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion
GOSPHIL311.contribution: examines historical and contemporary theories of emotion and their place in ethics, politics and art, supporting interpretation of cultural and philosophical texts

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: studies political thought from classical antiquity onward through original texts and historically situated arguments

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: develops empirical comparison of political institutions and democracy, complementing historical interpretations of ancient political communities

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: provides competing theories of interstate relations and case-based interpretation, complementing ancient conflict and political history without substituting for its sources

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: examines conflict, colonial legacies, identity and peacebuilding with interdisciplinary methods, providing a critical comparative perspective on political memory

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: examines social identities, boundaries, inequality and institutions, supporting interpretation of social groups and cultural selection

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: develops interviews, documentary inquiry, qualitative interpretation and reflexivity for research on public memory and cultural institutions

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: studies Greek and Roman rhetorical traditions and practices analysis of arguments and public speech

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.contribution: develops close linguistic and stylistic analysis of literary and non-fiction texts

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: studies persuasion, framing and ethical communication and tests public-facing interpretations through community projects

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.contribution: develops poetry, creative forms, revision and critically justified artistic choices, supporting the public and creative reception of cultural narratives

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: develops close visual analysis and contextual interpretation of Western art from the Renaissance onward, supporting comparison of later artistic traditions and heritage

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: interprets artefacts, technologies and craft organisation from the Neolithic through antiquity and practises archaeological recording and inference

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.contribution: examines African artistic traditions, colonial collecting and restitution, providing comparative analysis of heritage ownership and museum conflict

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: examines Renaissance Italian art and cross-Mediterranean exchange as a later cultural setting for interpreting classical legacies

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.contribution: studies material evidence of community and democracy in ancient Greece

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.contribution: examines museums, display choices and critical narratives of modern art, complementing the study of canon formation and public heritage

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.contribution: combines ancient Athenian history, archaeology, literature, religion and material sources to investigate democracy, exclusion and its modern uses

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: studies the history and methods of art history through influential texts and arguments about interpretation and cultural context

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: develops close reading, practical criticism and analysis of narrative, poetry and drama

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: compares ancient epic and Greek tragedy with later works through literary form, recurring motifs and cultural context

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: compares Greek, Roman, Near Eastern and other mythic traditions and their transmission, including creative reinterpretation of Ovid

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.contribution: studies adaptation, intertextuality and changes between literary narrative and film as methods for analysing reception

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.contribution: applies humanist, feminist, Marxist and other perspectives to literary meaning and research

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.contribution: develops formal and critical analysis of moving-image representation, supporting public presentation and interpretation of the past

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.contribution: examines media objects and infrastructures as material sources shaping knowledge and memory, a comparative material-culture method

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: studies racial construction, exclusion and marginalized storytelling through archives, media and participant inquiry, supporting critical reflection on cultural representation

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.contribution: develops documentary analysis and production, including research, interviewing and ethical choices in public representation

alignment.rationale: Both interpret material objects as evidence of past societies and develop archaeological documentation and inference.
Both investigate contested heritage, ownership and public narratives; UCR focuses on African art, colonial collections and restitution rather than the UNESCO framework.
Both examine later cultural uses and transformations of classical heritage; UCR concentrates on Renaissance visual culture and its wider connections.
Both use material evidence to study ancient Greek communities; the external survey also covers the Near East and a longer chronology.
Both examine cultural selection and the institutions and narratives that make works canonical; UCR focuses on modern art and museums.
Both examine participation, social groups and exclusion in ancient political life using textual and material evidence; UCR concentrates on Athens.
Both examine disciplinary methods, knowledge and interpretation in the humanities; UCR focuses on art history.
Both investigate empire, political power and decline with historical sources; UCR compares Rome with other ancient and later empires.
Both use theories of interstate relations to interpret political conflict; UCR uses modern cases while the external course works directly from ancient evidence.
Both develop interpretation of ancient philosophical arguments; UCR extends into later and contemporary philosophy.
Both interpret influential ancient literary works and their cultural significance; UCR also compares later works.
Both study Greek and Roman myth, its transmission and cultural interpretation; UCR compares further traditions.
Both develop creative writing, revision and critical justification of forms for a wider audience; UCR is not restricted to classical reception.
